deep.reconstruction:
Context: on 38v Gauss was building the numbers 1, 2, 2·8, 2·8·26, ... and similar sequences for other bases. On 39v he repeats the whole analysis for the base 1/2 and adds a continued fraction. This page treats base 1/3, i.e. q = 1/3 in modern q-series language.

(1) Product expansion. Let P(x) = ∏_{k≥1}(1 − x/3^k). Gauss writes
P(x) = 1 − x/2 + x²/(2·8) − x³/(2·8·26) + ...
In modern form this is P(x) = Σ_{n≥0} (−1)^n a_n x^n with a_n = 1/∏_{k=1}^{n}(3^k − 1). Equivalently a_n = q^{n(n+1)/2}/((1−q)...(1−q^n)) with q = 1/3, i.e. Euler's expansion of (xq;q)_∞.

(2) Logarithm. 'lP = ½x' is the first term of log P, started and then abandoned. The full series (my completion) is
log P = −Σ_m x^m/(m(3^m − 1)) = −(x/2 + x²/16 + x³/78 + ...).
Gauss writes the first term without the minus sign. On 39v he writes the analogous series for base 2 correctly, with the sign.

(3) Partial fractions of 1/P. Gauss writes
A/P = 1/(1 − x/3) − 1/(2(1 − x/9)) + 1/(2·8(1 − x/27)) − ...
so the partial-fraction coefficients of 1/P are exactly the coefficients (−1)^n a_n of P itself, attached to the pole at x = 3^{n+1}.
- Justification (mine): the residue at x = 3^{n+1} is 1/∏_{j≠n+1}(1 − 3^{n+1−j}), which equals (−1)^n a_n/Q with Q = ∏_{j≥1}(1 − 3^{−j}).
- Hence A = Q.
- Putting x = 0 gives A = 1 − 1/2 + 1/(2·8) − ... = P(1) = Q ≈ 0.56013, consistent. This is the 'Subtr. 1 − ½ + 1/(2·8) ...' line.

(4) Series of 1/P. In the right column Gauss writes
1/P = 1 + x/2 + (3/16)x² + 27/(2·8·26) x³ + ...
- In general the coefficient is b_n = 3^{n(n−1)/2}/∏_{k=1}^{n}(3^k − 1).
- The row '½, 3/8, 9/26, 27/80' gives the successive ratios b_n/b_{n−1} = 3^{n−1}/(3^n − 1).
- The scraps '3/32, 39, 1/32' are side arithmetic.

(5) Re-expanding the partial fractions. Gauss forms (1/P − 1)·A = A/P − A, which equals
Σ_n (−1)^n a_n (x/3^{n+1})/(1 − x/3^{n+1}) = (x/3)/(1 − x/3) − (x/9)/(2(1 − x/9)) + ...
- He then subtracts the linear terms x/3 − (x/9)/2 + ... = (x/3)·P(1/3).
- This leaves Σ (−1)^n a_n x² 3^{−2(n+1)}/(1 − x/3^{n+1}) = (x²/9)/(1 − x/3) − (x²/81)/(2(1 − x/9)) − ..., which is what he writes.
- Iterating, and writing (y) for the series 1 − y/2 + y²/(2·8) − ... = P(y), he obtains the final line
A/P − (1) − (x/3)(1/3) − (x²/9)(1/9) − (x³/27)(1/27) − ... = 0,
i.e. A/P(x) = Σ_{m≥0} (x/3)^m P(3^{−m}).
- Check (mine): P(3^{−m}) = Q/∏_{k=1}^{m}(1 − 3^{−k}) and A = Q. So this is equivalent to 1/P = Σ x^m 3^{−m}/∏_{k=1}^{m}(1 − 3^{−k}), which agrees with (4). The two expansions of 1/P are thus reconciled.

(6) Scratch work. The table '(1); (2)·1 − (1); (3)·1 − (2); (4) 1 − (3)' with x², x³ above it, and the expressions with α, β, γ, d at the bottom, are scratch. They are probably relations among the values (1), (1/3), (1/9), ... such as P(y) = (1 − y/3)P(y/3). Their exact content is not securely legible and I do not reconstruct them.
errors: 'lP = ½x' should be lP = −½x − ... (sign missing; the line is abandoned). On 39v Gauss writes the analogous series with the correct sign.
The left side of the fifth line is (1/P − 1)A (equivalently A/P − A), not '(A/P − 1)'. As written in the image it is consistent with the right-hand side.
No substantive errors otherwise. All displayed coefficients check: 1/2, 1/16, 1/416 for P; 1/2, 3/16, 27/416 for 1/P; ratios 1/2, 3/8, 9/26, 27/80.

results.modern_name: Euler's q-exponential identity / q-binomial theorem, special case q = 1/3
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Introductio, 1748); general q-binomial theorem to Gauss/Cauchy/Heine

results.what: Partial-fraction expansion of 1/∏(1−xq^k), whose coefficients are (up to the constant (q;q)_∞) the coefficients of the product itself
results.modern_name: Partial fraction expansion of 1/(xq;q)_∞, i.e. 1/(x;q)_∞ = (1/(q;q)_∞) Σ (−1)^n q^{n(n+1)/2}/((q;q)_n(1−xq^n))
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; appears in 19th-century q-series literature (Cauchy/Heine era) and in modern texts (Gasper–Rahman exercises)

results.what: Re-expansion A/P(x) = Σ (x/3)^m P(3^{−m}) with A = P(1) = ∏(1−3^{−k}), reconciling the partial-fraction and power-series forms
results.modern_name: Functional-equation / q-difference consequence of the product

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's extensive unpublished work on q-series (products ∏(1−xq^k), Gaussian binomials) is well known and partly printed in Werke III/X. The page is a careful special-case (q = 1/3) exploration of Euler's product–series identities. The partial-fraction expansion of 1/(xq;q)_∞ with coefficients mirroring the product's own coefficients is a nice, slightly non-routine observation, but it is classical and in keeping with his known interests.

checkable.sympy: series(Mul(*[1 - x/3**k for k in range(1,25)]), x, 0, 4)  # compare with 1 - x/2 + x**2/16 - x**3/416
checkable.asserts: P(x) = 1 - x/2 + x^2/(2*8) - x^3/(2*8*26) + ... (truncation error negligible)

checkable.sympy: series(1/Mul(*[1 - x/3**k for k in range(1,25)]), x, 0, 4)  # compare with 1 + x/2 + 3*x**2/16 + 27*x**3/416
a = lambda n: 1/prod([Integer(3)**k - 1 for k in range(1,n+1)]); N(sum((-1)**n*a(n) for n in range(30)) - prod([1 - Rational(1,3**k) for k in range(1,60)]))
xv = Rational(1,2); N(Q/prod([1 - xv/3**k for k in range(1,60)]) - sum((-1)**n*a(n)/(1 - xv/3**(n+1)) for n in range(30)))
checkable.asserts: Partial-fraction identity A/P(x) = sum (-1)^n a_n/(1 - x/3^(n+1)) at x = 1/2 (difference ≈ 0), with Q and a as defined above

checkable.sympy: Pf = lambda y: prod([1 - y/3**k for k in range(1,60)]); xv = Rational(1,2); N(Pf(1)/Pf(xv) - sum((xv/3)**m*Pf(Rational(1,3**m)) for m in range(40)))
checkable.asserts: Final line: A/P(x) = sum_m (x/3)^m P(3^-m) with A = P(1) (difference ≈ 0)
Ratios of successive coefficients of 1/P are 1/2, 3/8, 9/26, 27/80

transcription_corrections: 'lP = ½x': the image shows only the first term; the correct expansion begins −½x.
In the 'Subtr.' line the right-column series is the expansion of 1/P: 1 + ½x + 3/16 xx + 27/(2·8·26) x³; the fragments '3/32, 39, 1/32' are scratch arithmetic.
Final line: A/P − (1) − ⅓x(⅓) − 1/9 xx(1/9) − 1/27 x³(1/27) ... = 0, where (y) denotes the value of the series 1 − y/2 + y²/16 − ... at y.
